To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we introduce a novel approach for video recognition which learns to mine important visual tokens and efficiently processes such tokens for attention.

1) we introduce a novel adaptive tokenization method, which learns to mine a few important visual regions in images and videos and models the attention between them, and 2) we show that this method is competitive to the state-of-the-art, while being computationally more efficient.
we propose a novel visual representation for video recognition, and demonstrate its effectiveness and efficiency in several challenging tasks.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the question of how we can best learn visual representations in a data-efficient manner, while being robust to noise and robust to changes in visual content, such as the ones caused by changes in camera viewpoint or lighting.
developing a novel visual representation that can be efficiently and effectively learned from visual data.
developing a novel visual representation for video understanding.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we propose an approach to video understanding that relies on a handful (i.e., 32) of adaptively learned visual tokens, and which can be applied to a variety of tasks.

we have proposed an efficient and adaptive tokenization method that can be used in conjunction with existing self-supervised learning techniques, and that it outperforms existing state-of-the- arts on multiple video recognition benchmarks.

our method is able to learn a few adaptive and discriminative tokens, that are more informative than the original visual features, and that are able to capture the spatio-temporal dependencies in videos.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
our approach learns to adaptively split the video into a few tokens and then processes the tokens in a sequence.
we introduce the concept of adaptively learned tokenization, which can be used for a wide range of computer vision tasks.
we propose a novel approach for learning visual tokens from video data, which is adaptive, and which can be applied to both image and videos.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a handful of adaptatively learned tokens are sufficient for learning powerful visual representations.
a small number of adaptively learned visual tokens, when used to model attention over the spatial and temporal content, can achieve state-of-the-art performance for video understanding tasks.
a few adaptive tokens can effectively model the visual content, and the learned tokenization can be transferred to different tasks.
